body.heading: Look at the ground
paragraphs: Animals leave clues where they walk. On soft mud, sand, or snow, their feet press shapes into the ground. These shapes are called tracks.
Walk slowly with your adult and look down. A good place to look is the edge of a puddle or a muddy path after rain.

body.heading: Be a detective
paragraphs: When you find a track, stop and look. How many toes can you see? Is it big or small? Does it have claw marks?
Draw the track in your notebook the same size as the real one. Your adult can write down where and when you found it. Guessing which animal made it is part of the fun, and it is fine to be unsure.

body.heading: Follow the story, not the animal
paragraphs: Tracks tell a story: something walked here, stopped, then hurried away. You can follow the story for a few steps.
Never follow an animal itself, and never touch a wild animal. Detectives watch and wonder; they do not chase.

description: For ages 6–9 with an adult: look for footprints in mud or snow and guess which animal passed by.

safetyNotes: Stay with your adult on paths, watch for slippery mud, and wash hands when you get home.
Never touch or follow a wild animal; only look at the tracks it left behind.

takeaway: Every footprint is a clue that an animal was here before you.
